title: Selling an Inherited Home: Where to Start
excerpt: Selling a home you've inherited is a different process from a typical sale, emotionally and legally. Here's how to approach it.
content:
Selling a home you've inherited is rarely simple. Beyond the emotional weight of it, there are real legal and practical steps that differ from a typical sale, and getting the order of operations right matters.

**Start With the Legal Basics**
Before a home can be sold, ownership needs to be legally clear. In Massachusetts, this often involves the probate process, where a court confirms the will (or applies state law if there isn't one) and appoints an executor or personal representative with legal authority to act on the estate's behalf, including selling real estate. Until that authority is established, a sale generally can't move forward. This is a good reason to loop in a probate or estate attorney early, before you start thinking about listing timelines.

**Get Clear on Ownership Among Heirs**
If the home is inherited by multiple people, siblings, for example, everyone with an ownership stake needs to agree on selling, and ideally agree on the basics: timeline, [listing price expectations](/sell), and how proceeds will be divided. Disagreements among heirs are one of the most common things that stall an inherited home sale, so it's worth having that conversation directly and early, separate from the emotions of the loss itself.

**Understand the Tax Basics**
Inherited property generally receives what's called a "stepped-up basis," meaning the property's value is reset to its fair market value at the time of the original owner's passing, rather than what they originally paid for it decades earlier. This can significantly reduce capital gains taxes if you sell relatively soon after inheriting. The specifics depend on your situation, so this is worth a conversation with a tax professional or estate attorney rather than assuming, but it's an important reason not to delay the conversation.

**Decide: Sell, Rent, or Keep**
Before assuming a sale is the right move, it's worth briefly considering the alternatives:
- Selling provides a clean break and immediate liquidity, especially useful when multiple heirs need to divide proceeds
- Renting can make sense if the home has strong long-term value and someone is willing to manage it as a landlord
- Keeping the home in the family works when one heir wants to live in it and can buy out the others' shares

Most families land on selling, but it's worth a genuine conversation rather than defaulting to it.

**Preparing the Home**
Inherited homes have often been lived in for decades, sometimes with deferred maintenance the previous owner didn't get to. A few practical steps:
- Clearing out personal belongings, often the most emotionally difficult and time-consuming step
- An honest [inspection](/blog/home-inspection-massachusetts) to understand what condition the home is actually in
- Deciding how much, if any, [updating makes sense before listing](/blog/home-improvements-that-add-value) versus selling as-is

Selling as-is is a completely reasonable choice for an inherited home, particularly when heirs want to move quickly or don't want to manage a renovation from a distance.

**Frequently Asked Questions**

Do I need to go through probate to sell an inherited home? In most cases, yes. An executor or personal representative typically needs legal authority through the probate process before a sale can close. An estate attorney can confirm what applies to your specific situation.

What if my siblings and I disagree about selling? This is common, and worth resolving directly and early, ideally with guidance from an attorney or mediator, since it can otherwise stall the process indefinitely.

Will I owe a lot of capital gains tax on an inherited home? Often less than people expect, thanks to the stepped-up basis, but the specifics depend on your situation. A tax professional can give you a real answer.

Should I renovate before selling an inherited home? Not necessarily. Many inherited homes sell successfully as-is, particularly when heirs want a simpler, faster process.

title: New Construction vs. an Older New England Home: What You're Really Trading Off
seoTitle: New Construction vs. an Older New England Home
excerpt: New builds and 100-year-old Colonials solve different problems. Here's what actually differs day to day, beyond just age.
content:
Greater Boston is unusual in how much of its housing stock predates modern construction entirely. It's not uncommon to tour homes built in the 1800s alongside listings finished last year. The choice between them isn't really about "old vs. new" as a preference. It's a set of concrete tradeoffs worth understanding before you commit.

**What You Get With an Older Home**
Established towns across the region built their character around homes that have been there for generations. That tends to come with:
- Mature trees, established landscaping, and often larger lots than newer developments
- Walkable proximity to [historic town centers](/blog/why-new-england-towns-arent-like-anywhere-else), which were built around the homes, not the other way around
- Architectural character, like real plaster walls, original woodwork, and unique layouts, that's difficult or expensive to replicate in new construction
- Often, a lower price per square foot than comparable new construction in the same town

**What You're Signing Up For**
Older homes also come with predictable tradeoffs:
- Systems (electrical, plumbing, heating) that may need updating even if they're currently functional
- Smaller closets, choppier floor plans, and less of the open-concept layout many buyers now expect
- A higher likelihood of needing a specialist for issues like [lead paint, asbestos, or an aging oil tank](/blog/home-inspection-massachusetts)
- Ongoing maintenance that a newer home simply doesn't require yet

**What You Get With New Construction**
Newer homes solve a different set of problems:
- Modern, efficient systems, from heating to insulation to electrical, that lower both maintenance costs and energy bills
- Open floor plans, larger closets, and layouts designed around how people actually live today
- A builder warranty covering workmanship and major systems for roughly the first year
- Little to no deferred maintenance to inherit from a previous owner

**What New Construction Trades Away**
The tradeoffs run the other direction too:
- New developments are often located farther from historic town centers and transit than older housing stock
- Lot sizes tend to be smaller, and mature landscaping takes years to develop
- Character and uniqueness are harder to come by — new construction often follows a more standardized design
- Depending on the town, inventory of true new construction can be limited, since much of the region is already built out

**How to Actually Decide**
The honest framing: an older home is buying into an established place, with all its character and its maintenance needs. New construction is buying predictability and modern living, often at the cost of location and character. Neither is objectively right. It depends on whether you're the type of buyer who wants to spend a weekend refinishing original hardwood, or the type who'd rather never think about a furnace for the first decade.

**Frequently Asked Questions**

Is new construction always more expensive? Not always. It depends on the town and lot, but new construction often does carry a premium per square foot compared to an older home in the same area, partly for the reduced maintenance risk.

Are older homes in Greater Boston hard to insure? Not necessarily, but insurers may ask more questions about the age of the electrical panel, roof, and heating system — items worth addressing if they haven't been updated.

Do new construction homes hold value as well as older homes in established towns? Both can appreciate well; it tends to depend more on the town and [school district](/blog/top-school-districts-metrowest) than on the age of the specific home.

Can I get the character of an older home with fewer of the maintenance headaches? Sometimes — a home that's already been [thoughtfully renovated](/blog/fixer-upper-or-move-in-ready) by a previous owner can offer a middle ground worth looking for.

title: When to Upsize: The Real Signs Your Home No Longer Fits
excerpt: Upsizing is about more than square footage. Here's how to know your current home has actually become a constraint.
content:
Upsizing decisions often get reduced to "we need another bedroom." But the real signs your home no longer fits are usually broader than that, and catching them early makes the eventual move much less stressful.

**Signs You've Actually Outgrown Your Home**
A few patterns come up again and again with families who end up upsizing:
- Hosting family or friends immediately exposes the constraints: no guest room, kids doubling up, everyone tripping over each other
- Kids who used to share a room are getting older and need their own space, not as a luxury but for basic privacy
- You're using improvised spaces, like a dining table as a desk or a hallway as storage, because there's no dedicated room for how you actually live
- Storage has become a constant stress, not an occasional inconvenience
- Remote or hybrid work has made a dedicated office a genuine need, not a nice-to-have

These patterns tend to compound over time rather than resolve on their own.

**It's Not Just About Bedroom Count**
Two homes with the same number of bedrooms can feel completely different in practice. A home that's technically "big enough" on paper but has an awkward layout, with bedrooms too close together, no separation between living and work space, and a kitchen that can't handle how your household actually cooks and gathers, can feel more cramped than a smaller home with a layout that actually matches your life.

**Financial Readiness for an Upsize**
Before starting the search, it's worth getting clear on:
- [How much equity your current home has built](/sell), and what that gives you toward a larger purchase
- Whether you'll need to sell before buying, or have the flexibility to buy first, since this affects both your timeline and your negotiating position
- What your realistic budget looks like once you factor in a larger home's [higher property taxes, utilities, and maintenance costs](/mortgage), not just the purchase price

**Timing the Sale and Purchase**
One of the more stressful parts of upsizing is coordinating the sale of your current home with the purchase of your next one. A few common approaches:
- Selling first, then renting or staying with family temporarily while you search: lower financial risk, but less convenient
- Making a contingent offer on your next home, tied to the sale of your current one: more convenient, but can make your offer less competitive in a competitive listing
- Buying first and selling your current home after: for buyers in a strong financial position, this is a strategy we often recommend, since it means you're never rushed on either side of the transaction and you can move once, not twice

If you buy before selling, a HELOC (home equity line of credit) on your current home is a common way to access the equity you've already built for a down payment on the next one, without waiting for your current home to close first. It's not the right fit for everyone. It depends on your equity position and comfort carrying two properties briefly, but for the right buyer it's one of the smoothest ways to upsize.

There's no universally right approach. It depends on your risk tolerance, your current home's likely time on market, and how competitive the town you're moving to happens to be.

**What to Prioritize in the Next Home**
It's easy to upsize into "more of the same, but bigger." Instead, it's worth getting specific about what was actually constraining you, whether it was bedrooms, storage, a dedicated workspace, entertaining space, or a yard, and prioritizing that directly, rather than just square footage in general.

A useful exercise before you start touring homes: walk through your current one room by room and write down exactly where it falls short. Not "we need more space," but specifics like "no place for overnight guests" or "the kids have been sharing a room for two years and it's not working anymore." That list becomes your actual search criteria, and it'll keep you from paying for square footage that doesn't solve the problem you started with.

**Frequently Asked Questions**

How do I know if we need more space or just better-organized space? Reorganizing can help at the margins, but if you've already decluttered and it's still not enough, if hosting family reliably feels tight, or the kids need their own rooms and there's nowhere to put them, that's not a storage problem. That's a home that's structurally too small for how your family lives now.

Should I sell my current home before buying the next one? It depends on your risk tolerance and the markets on both ends. Selling first reduces financial risk; buying first (if you can manage it) reduces the stress of a rushed search.

What if we can't agree on how much space we actually need? Walking through specific scenarios, like where a home office would go or where overnight guests would stay, often clarifies this faster than an abstract conversation about square footage.

Should we look to upsize in our current town, or is it worth considering somewhere new? Both are common, and it comes down to what's driving the move. If your town and school district are already working well for your family, staying local while sizing up is usually the simplest path. But since you're moving anyway, it's worth at least evaluating whether a [neighboring town](/neighborhoods) might better match what you need next: more land, a shorter commute, or a school district that's an even better fit as your kids get older.

title: Best Weekend Day Trips from Greater Boston
excerpt: One of the underrated perks of living here: an enormous range of genuinely great day trips within an hour or two of almost anywhere in the region.
content:
Part of what makes living in Greater Boston appealing isn't just the region itself. It's everything within easy reach of it. Few U.S. metro areas pack this much variety, coastline, mountains, historic towns, classic New England charm, into a couple hours' drive. Here's what regularly makes the list for people who live here.

**Cape Cod**
The classic New England summer day trip (or weekend, if you can swing it). Beaches, seafood, small coastal towns, and the Cape Cod Rail Trail for anyone who wants to bring a bike along. It gets crowded in peak summer, but a shoulder-season trip in late spring or early fall is one of the best-kept secrets of living in this region. The [Cape Cod Chamber of Commerce](https://www.capecodchamber.org) site is a good starting point for planning.

**Salem**
Best known for its history, both the witch trials and its long maritime past, Salem makes for an easy half-day or full-day trip, especially rich for anyone with kids old enough to be interested in history. It's also a genuinely walkable, well-preserved small city worth seeing beyond the October crowds. [Destination Salem](https://www.salem.org) has the full rundown of what's open and worth seeing.

**Concord and Lexington**
You don't have to leave the immediate area for a great day trip. [Concord](/neighborhoods/concord) and [Lexington](/neighborhoods/lexington), both towns we work in regularly, are worth a dedicated day even for people who've lived nearby for years. Walden Pond, the Old North Bridge, and the Battle Road historic sites pack a genuine sense of place into a short drive from almost anywhere in Greater Boston.

**Newport, Rhode Island**
About an hour and a half south, Newport offers the Gilded Age mansions along Bellevue Avenue, the Cliff Walk along the coastline, and a genuinely charming harbor town center. It's a bit further than some of the others on this list, but consistently rated as one of the best day trips (or overnight trips) from the Boston area. [Discover Newport](https://www.discovernewport.org) has mansion tickets and Cliff Walk details.

**Portsmouth, New Hampshire**
A little over an hour north, Portsmouth offers a walkable historic downtown, a strong local restaurant scene, and easy access to the New Hampshire seacoast: a nice change of pace without needing a full weekend to make it worthwhile.

**Plymouth**
Closer to home, Plymouth offers a manageable half-day trip focused on the town's role in early American history, along with a working waterfront that makes for a pleasant afternoon regardless of your interest in the historical sites specifically. [See Plymouth](https://www.seeplymouth.com) is the local tourism site for hours and events.

**The Berkshires**
For a trip that requires a bit more commitment, roughly two and a half hours west, the Berkshires offer a completely different New England experience: mountains, hiking, and a surprisingly strong arts and culture scene. Best suited to an actual weekend rather than a single day, but worth the drive. [1Berkshire](https://www.1berkshire.com) is a good resource for planning.

**Why This Is Worth Mentioning to Buyers**
For people relocating from areas without this kind of regional variety, it's easy to underestimate how much day-trip access adds to quality of life here. It's a genuine answer to "what do people actually do for fun" beyond the towns themselves, and it's worth factoring in alongside [schools and commute time](/blog/boston-vs-suburbs) when you're evaluating whether this region is the right fit for your family.

**Frequently Asked Questions**

What's the best day trip for families with young kids? Salem and Plymouth both work well: manageable drive times, walkable town centers, and genuinely engaging history for kids.

Is Cape Cod worth visiting outside of summer? Many locals actually prefer it in late spring or early fall: fewer crowds, still very pleasant weather, and easier restaurant reservations.

How far is too far for a single-day trip? Most of the destinations here are under two hours each way, which keeps a day trip genuinely enjoyable rather than mostly spent driving. The Berkshires are the exception, better suited to a weekend.

Do any of these make sense as a short overnight rather than a day trip? Newport, the Berkshires, and Cape Cod are all strong overnight options if you want to slow the pace down rather than rushing back the same day.

title: Should You Keep Your Low-Rate Home or Sell It?
excerpt: Many homeowners are holding on to a low mortgage rate, some by keeping the old home as a rental. Here's how to tell whether keeping it actually pays.
content:
If you bought or refinanced when mortgage rates were near historic lows, selling can feel like giving up something you'll never get back. That's why many homeowners are staying put instead of moving, and why others who do move keep the old home and rent it out. Holding on to a low rate can be the right call. But a low rate on its own doesn't make a home a good investment, and many owners who turn their old home into a rental find it costs them money every month, even with a tenant in it.

**Why Low-Rate Homeowners Are Holding On**
The reasoning feels simple: a mortgage at a rate well below today's is cheap money, and a new mortgage on the next home will cost more. So owners either stay longer than they planned, or move and keep the first home as a rental, expecting the rent to cover the mortgage while the home keeps appreciating.

**Where the Rental Math Often Falls Short**
Rent covering the mortgage payment isn't the same as the property paying for itself. Once the home becomes a rental, the full monthly cost usually includes:
- The mortgage payment itself
- Property taxes, which can rise once it's no longer your primary residence. In Boston and the other Massachusetts communities that offer a residential exemption, it only applies to owner-occupied homes, so a converted rental loses it
- Landlord insurance, which typically costs more than a homeowner's policy
- Repairs and maintenance, which don't stop because someone else lives there, and tenants expect them handled quickly
- Vacancy and turnover between tenants, including cleaning, painting, and lost rent
- Property management fees if you hire someone, or your own time if you don't
- Broker fees: since August 1, 2025, a Massachusetts landlord who hires a broker to find a tenant pays that fee, instead of passing it on to the tenant

Add those up and many owners find the rent covers most of the cost, but not all of it, so they're paying the difference out of pocket every month. That can still be worth it as a long-term investment, but it's worth knowing the number before you decide, not after.

**The Equity You're Not Using**
A low rate is only part of the picture. If your home has gained significant value, that equity stays in the old house instead of going toward your next one. That means a smaller down payment and a bigger mortgage at today's rates on the new home, which can offset much of what you save by keeping the low rate.

Here's an example with round numbers. Say your current home is worth $800,000, you owe $350,000 on a 3% mortgage, and you're buying a $1,000,000 home with a new mortgage at 6.5%:
- Keep the old home: you put 20% down from savings ($200,000) and borrow $800,000. Principal and interest on the new home comes to about $5,057 a month.
- Sell the old home: after paying off the $350,000 mortgage and about $50,000 in selling costs, you walk away with roughly $400,000. Put that down and you borrow $600,000, about $3,792 a month in principal and interest, and your $200,000 in savings stays in the bank.

That's about $1,264 more every month, or roughly $255,000 more in interest over 30 years, just from borrowing the $200,000 that's tied up in the old house. And that's before any monthly shortfall on the rental itself.

Keeping the home does have upside: you still own an appreciating asset, and the rent pays down a loan at 3%. The question is whether that return is worth more to you than the higher payment on the home you actually live in. Every $100,000 you borrow at 6.5% adds about $632 a month to a 30-year mortgage, so you can run the same math with your own numbers in our [mortgage calculator](/mortgage).

Some owners tap that equity with a HELOC instead, but that's new debt at today's rates too.

**Taxes to Know Before You Convert**
- The capital gains exclusion: when you sell a home you've lived in as your primary residence for at least 2 of the last 5 years, up to $250,000 of gain ($500,000 for married couples filing jointly) is generally tax-free. Rent it out for more than about three years after moving out, and you can lose that exclusion.
- Depreciation recapture: once it's a rental, the depreciation you claimed, or were entitled to claim, is generally taxed when you sell, even if the rest of the gain is excluded.
- Rental income and expenses are reported on your tax return every year.

A tax professional can tell you how these apply to your situation before you decide.

**Being a Landlord in Massachusetts**
Massachusetts rental rules are among the more tenant-protective in the country, so it's worth knowing the basics before you become a landlord:
- Security deposits must be held in a separate, interest-bearing account at a Massachusetts bank, with specific paperwork, and mistakes can cost you several times the deposit
- If a child under 6 lives in a home built before 1978, the lead law requires it to be deleaded
- Evictions go through the courts and can take months
- Check your mortgage terms, since many loans require you to live in the home for at least the first year, and switch to a landlord insurance policy before your first tenant moves in

**When Keeping the Home Makes Sense**
- The rent covers all of the costs, not just the mortgage, or you're comfortable covering a modest gap as a long-term investment
- You have cash reserves to handle a vacancy or a major repair
- You can buy your next home without the equity in this one
- You want to be a landlord, or are willing to pay a property manager
- You expect to move back, or plan to hold the home for many years

**When Selling Makes More Sense**
- The home costs you money every month even with a tenant in it, and you don't see that changing
- You need the equity for your next down payment
- You don't want the responsibility of tenants, repairs, and turnover
- You're approaching three years since you moved out and want to keep the capital gains exclusion

**A Simple Way to Run the Numbers**
1. Estimate realistic rent, based on what comparable homes nearby have actually rented for.
2. Add up the full monthly cost: mortgage, taxes, landlord insurance, and set-asides for maintenance, vacancy, and management.
3. Subtract the cost from the rent. If the result is negative, that's what holding the home costs you each month.
4. Weigh that against what selling would free up: your equity, a smaller mortgage on the next home, and a tax-free gain if you sell within the exclusion window.

Our [mortgage calculator](/mortgage) helps with the monthly payment side, and a [home valuation](/sell) shows what your equity looks like today.

**Frequently Asked Questions**

Is it smart to keep a low-rate home and rent it out? It can be, if the rent covers all the costs, not just the mortgage, and you're prepared for vacancies, repairs, and the work of being a landlord. If it costs you money every month, you're essentially paying to hold on to the low rate.

How long can I rent out my old home and still avoid capital gains tax when I sell? Generally, the exclusion applies if you lived in the home for at least 2 of the 5 years before the sale, which gives you up to about three years after moving out. Depreciation recapture still applies to the rental period, so confirm the details with a tax professional.

Can I take my low mortgage rate with me to a new home? Generally no, since a mortgage is tied to the property. Some loans, including FHA and VA loans, can be assumed by a qualified buyer with the lender's approval, which can make your home more attractive when you sell.

Do I need to tell my lender if I turn my home into a rental? Check your mortgage terms. Many loans require you to live in the home for at least the first year. After that, converting is common, but you should also switch to a landlord insurance policy.

What if I'm not sure I want to sell yet? Run the numbers first. Knowing exactly what the home would cost you to hold each month, and what selling would free up, usually makes the decision much clearer.

title: Should You Buy a Home Now or Wait for Mortgage Rates to Drop?
excerpt: It's one of the most-asked questions in real estate right now. Here's how to think it through without trying to predict the market.
content:
It's one of the most common questions buyers ask right now: should I buy now, or wait until mortgage rates come down? It's a reasonable question, but it's built on a prediction nobody can make reliably. Not economists, not lenders, and not agents. A better approach is to decide based on what you can actually know: your finances, your timeline, and what's happening in the towns you're considering.

**Why Waiting Isn't Automatically the Safer Choice**
Waiting for lower rates assumes two things: that rates will fall, and that nothing else will change while you wait. Neither is guaranteed. If rates do drop, more buyers typically come back into the market at the same time, which can mean more competition for the same limited number of homes. In much of Greater Boston, where inventory has been tight for years, more competition can push prices up and make it harder to win a home on reasonable terms.

Waiting also has its own costs. Every month you rent is a month of payments that don't build equity, and life events, like a growing family, a new job, or a school year starting, don't wait for the rate environment.

**Why Buying Now Isn't Automatically Right Either**
None of this means you should rush. Buying before you're ready, financially or personally, is a bigger risk than paying a somewhat higher rate. If the monthly payment at today's rates would stretch your budget, or you're not confident you'll stay in the area for at least a few years, waiting can be the right call for reasons that have nothing to do with rates.

**The Questions That Actually Decide It**
- Can you comfortably afford the monthly payment at today's rates, without counting on a future refinance?
- Do you have your down payment and closing costs saved, with an emergency fund still intact afterward?
- Do you plan to stay in the home long enough for the upfront costs of buying to pay for themselves, typically several years?
- Is your job and income stable enough to take on a mortgage now?
- Have you found towns and homes that fit what you need, not just your budget?

If the answer to all of these is yes, the rate environment matters less than it feels like it does.

**What About Refinancing Later?**
Many buyers plan to buy now and refinance if rates drop. That can work, but treat it as a possible bonus, not the plan. Refinancing has its own closing costs, requires you to qualify again, and depends on rates falling enough to make the math work. Choose a payment you can live with at today's rate, and if a refinance makes sense later, that's a win.

**Ways to Manage the Rate You Get**
- Shop more than one lender. Rates and fees can differ meaningfully for the same borrower.
- Ask about buying down your rate with points, and compare what you'd pay upfront against what you'd save each month.
- Ask sellers about concessions toward your closing costs or a rate buydown, which can be more valuable to you than a lower price.
- Look at different loan types. An adjustable-rate mortgage can make sense for some buyers who expect to move or refinance within the fixed period, as long as they understand how the rate can change afterward.

Our [mortgage calculator](/mortgage) lets you see how the monthly payment changes at different rates and prices.

**Frequently Asked Questions**

Will home prices drop if I wait? No one can say for sure. In much of Greater Boston, limited inventory has kept prices high even as rates rose, so waiting for both lower rates and lower prices is a bet on two things at once. Our [market report](/market) shows how prices and days on market have moved over the past year.

Is it better to buy with a higher rate or wait for a lower one? It depends on your situation, not the market. If you're financially ready and plan to stay put, buying at a payment you can afford is usually more important than timing the rate.

How much does a 1% difference in rate actually change my payment? It depends on the loan amount. On a larger loan, it can mean several hundred dollars a month, which is why it's worth running your own numbers in a mortgage calculator rather than relying on rules of thumb.

Should I wait until spring to buy? Spring usually brings more listings, but also more buyers. Fall and winter often have less competition, and motivated sellers. A well-prepared buyer can find the right home in any season.

title: How Much Does It Cost to Sell a Home in Massachusetts?
excerpt: From the deed excise tax to your attorney and agent, here's what Massachusetts sellers actually pay, and what to budget before you list.
content:
When you sell a home, the sale price isn't what you walk away with. Between commissions, taxes, fees, and preparation costs, the total cost of selling usually adds up to a meaningful share of the price. Knowing the numbers ahead of time helps you set realistic expectations and plan your next move. Here's what Massachusetts sellers typically pay.

**Real Estate Commissions**
Commission is usually the largest selling cost. It's always negotiable and not set by law, and it should be discussed and agreed on in writing before you list. Since practice changes in August 2024, offers to pay a buyer's agent can no longer be advertised on MLS listings. As a seller, you decide whether to offer compensation to a buyer's agent, or to consider it if a buyer asks for it in their offer. Talk through those options with your listing agent before you go to market.

**The Massachusetts Deed Excise Tax**
Massachusetts charges a deed excise tax, often called "tax stamps," when a property sells, and by custom the seller pays it. The rate is $4.56 per $1,000 of the sale price across Greater Boston and most of the state. On an $800,000 sale, that's $3,648. Barnstable County (Cape Cod) charges a higher rate.

**Attorney Fees**
In Massachusetts, closings are handled by attorneys. Most sellers hire their own attorney to prepare the deed, review the Purchase and Sale Agreement, and handle payoffs and closing documents. Fees vary, so ask for a quote up front.

**Paying Off Your Mortgage**
Your mortgage and any home equity line of credit are paid off at closing from the sale proceeds. The payoff includes interest through the closing date, and there's a small fee to record the discharge of the mortgage. Ask your lender for a payoff estimate early so there are no surprises.

**Massachusetts-Specific Requirements**
- Smoke and carbon monoxide certificate: before closing, the local fire department inspects the detectors and issues a certificate, for a fee set by each town
- Title 5 septic inspection: required for homes with a septic system, with the cost depending on the system
- Condo 6(d) certificate: if you're selling a condo, the association issues a certificate confirming your condo fees are paid up, and may charge a fee for it

**Adjustments at Closing**
Property taxes, water and sewer charges, and sometimes fuel oil in the tank are prorated between buyer and seller at closing, so you'll either pay or receive the difference depending on what's already been paid.

**Preparing the Home**
Pre-listing costs are optional but often pay for themselves: fresh paint, deep cleaning, minor repairs, landscaping, and staging. Our guide to [improvements that actually add value](/blog/home-improvements-that-add-value) covers where that money is best spent.

**Negotiated Costs**
After the buyer's [inspection](/blog/home-inspection-massachusetts), you may agree to repairs or a credit at closing. Buyers sometimes also ask for help with their closing costs. These are negotiated, not required, but they're worth budgeting for.

**Moving and the Overlap Between Homes**
Don't forget the cost of the move itself, and any period where you're carrying two homes, renting short-term, or storing belongings between closings.

**Capital Gains Taxes**
Most homeowners selling a primary residence owe little or no capital gains tax: if you've lived in the home for at least 2 of the last 5 years, up to $250,000 of gain ($500,000 for married couples filing jointly) is generally excluded. Gains above that, or on a home that wasn't your primary residence, may be taxable at both the federal and state level. A tax professional can tell you what applies to you.

**A Simple Way to Estimate Your Net Proceeds**
Start with your expected sale price, then subtract your mortgage payoff, commission, deed excise tax, attorney fee, and an allowance for preparation, repairs or credits, and moving. A [home valuation](/sell) based on recent sales nearby gives you a realistic starting point for the sale price.

**Frequently Asked Questions**

Who pays the transfer tax in Massachusetts, buyer or seller? By custom, the seller pays the deed excise tax, at $4.56 per $1,000 of the sale price in most of the state.

Are real estate commissions negotiable? Yes. Commissions are not set by law, and the terms are agreed on in writing between you and your agent.

Do I need a lawyer to sell a house in Massachusetts? Closings in Massachusetts are conducted by attorneys, and most sellers hire their own attorney to represent them.

When do I get the money from my sale? Proceeds are typically disbursed at or shortly after closing, once the deed is recorded and your mortgage is paid off.

title: ADUs in Massachusetts: What Homeowners Can Build Now
excerpt: Since February 2025, most Massachusetts homeowners can add an accessory dwelling unit without a special permit. Here's what the law allows and what to know first.
content:
An accessory dwelling unit, or ADU, is a small, self-contained home on the same lot as a single-family house: an in-law apartment, a unit over the garage, or a backyard cottage. Until recently, most Massachusetts towns made them hard or impossible to build. That changed with the state's Affordable Homes Act, and it's opened up new options for homeowners who want space for aging parents, adult kids, or rental income.

**What Changed**
Since February 2, 2025, Massachusetts allows one ADU "by right" on lots in single-family zoning districts. By right means you don't need a special permit, a variance, or a public hearing for a qualifying ADU, as long as it meets the state's standards and reasonable local rules. The law applies to every city and town except Boston, which has its own ADU rules.

**The Basic Requirements**
- Size: the ADU can be no larger than 900 square feet, or half the gross floor area of the main house, whichever is smaller
- One by right: one ADU per lot is allowed by right; additional units still need local approval
- Attached or detached: it can be part of the main house, like a basement or attic apartment, or a separate building on the lot
- Building code: the ADU has to meet the same building, health, and safety codes as any other home

Towns can still apply reasonable rules on things like setbacks and design, so check with your local building department before you plan. If your home has a septic system, its capacity can also limit what you can add.

**Paying for an ADU**
Building an ADU is a real construction project, and costs vary widely depending on whether you're converting existing space or building something new. Since spring 2026, MassHousing has offered an ADU loan program for income-eligible homeowners, with second mortgages of up to $250,000 for a detached ADU or $150,000 for an attached one, for homeowners who already have their designs and permits in hand. Program details can change, so check [MassHousing](https://www.masshousing.com) for current terms. Many homeowners also use a home equity line of credit or a renovation loan.

**Why Homeowners Are Building Them**
- Multigenerational living: a parent can live close by with their own space and privacy
- Adult children: a way to give young adults an affordable start without sharing a kitchen
- Rental income: a long-term rental can help offset your mortgage and property taxes
- Aging in place: some homeowners build an ADU to move into themselves and rent or give the main house to family

**What to Think About Before You Build**
- Your budget, including design, permitting, utilities, and site work, not just construction
- How it affects your property taxes, since an ADU adds assessed value
- Your homeowner's insurance, which will need to cover the new unit
- If you plan to rent it out, Massachusetts landlord rules, including how security deposits must be handled
- How it fits your lot: setbacks, parking, access, and privacy for both households

**Does an ADU Add Value?**
An ADU can make a home more appealing to buyers looking for multigenerational space or income potential. How much value it adds depends on the town, the quality of the unit, and how it fits the property, so it's worth looking at recent sales of homes with ADUs nearby before assuming a return. If you're thinking about buying a home with an existing ADU, our [town guides](/neighborhoods) are a good place to compare areas.

**Frequently Asked Questions**

Do I need a special permit to build an ADU in Massachusetts? Not for a qualifying ADU in a single-family zoning district outside Boston. You'll still need a building permit and must meet code and reasonable local requirements.

How big can an ADU be? Up to 900 square feet, or half the gross floor area of the main house, whichever is smaller.

Can I rent out my ADU? Generally, yes, as a long-term rental, but check your town's rules, since some communities restrict short-term rentals.

Does the ADU law apply in Boston? No. Boston is exempt from the state law and has its own ADU program and rules.

title: Buying a Condo in Massachusetts: What to Check Before You Buy
excerpt: With a condo, you're buying into an association as well as a unit. Here's what to look at before you make an offer.
content:
Condos are often the most accessible way to buy in Greater Boston, especially in and around the city, and they come with real advantages: less maintenance, often a better location for the price, and someone else handling the roof and the snow. But when you buy a condo, you're buying into an association too. Its finances, rules, and condition affect your costs and your experience as much as the unit itself.

**What Your Condo Fee Covers**
Condo fees, also called common charges, vary widely, and so does what they include. Before comparing two condos on fee alone, find out what each one covers:
- Building insurance, exterior maintenance, and common area upkeep
- Snow removal and landscaping
- Water and sewer, heat, or hot water in some buildings
- Contributions to the reserve fund for future repairs

A lower fee isn't always a better deal if it means the association isn't saving enough for the big-ticket items ahead.

**Reserves and Special Assessments**
Every building eventually needs a new roof, new windows, masonry work, or a new boiler. A healthy association saves for those through a reserve fund. If reserves are thin, owners can be hit with a special assessment, a one-time charge that can run into the thousands. Ask for the association's budget, its current reserve balance, and whether any special assessments are planned or being discussed.

**Small Associations**
Much of Greater Boston's condo housing is in converted two- and three-family homes, where the "association" is just you and one or two neighbors. These can work very well, but they're often self-managed, with smaller reserves and decisions that depend on everyone agreeing. Ask how decisions are made, how expenses are split, and whether there's any written budget or reserve at all.

**The Documents to Review**
- The master deed, declaration of trust, and bylaws, which set the rules
- Rules and regulations, including pets, rentals, renovations, and parking
- The current budget and the most recent financial statements
- Minutes from recent association meetings, which often reveal upcoming projects, disputes, or assessments
- The master insurance policy

Your attorney will review the legal documents, but read the meeting minutes and budget yourself. They tell you a lot about how the building is run.

**Insurance**
The association's master policy covers the building and common areas. You'll also need your own condo policy, often called an HO-6, to cover your unit's interior, your belongings, and liability. Ask what the master policy's deductible is, since owners can be responsible for part of it after a claim.

**Financing a Condo**
Lenders look at the association as well as you. Things like the share of units that are owner-occupied, the association's reserves, and any pending litigation can affect your financing options. If you're using an FHA or VA loan, the condo may need to meet that program's requirements. Ask your lender early in your search, not after you've made an offer.

**The 6(d) Certificate**
At closing, Massachusetts law provides for a 6(d) certificate from the association, confirming whether the seller owes any unpaid condo fees or assessments. It protects you from inheriting someone else's unpaid charges. Your attorney will make sure it's in place.

**The Unit Itself**
A home [inspection](/blog/home-inspection-massachusetts) still matters for a condo. The inspector will focus on your unit's systems, like the electrical, plumbing, heating and cooling, and windows, and can flag visible issues with common areas that are worth asking the association about.

**Frequently Asked Questions**

Are condo fees tax deductible? Not for a home you live in. They can be deductible as an expense if you rent the unit out.

Can condo fees go up? Yes. Fees are set by the association's annual budget and can rise with costs like insurance, utilities, and repairs.

Can I rent out my condo? It depends on the association's rules. Some limit or prohibit rentals, or require a minimum lease term, so check the documents before you buy if renting might be part of your plans.

Is a condo a good first home? It can be: less maintenance, often a better location for the price, and a way to start building equity. Just make sure the association is financially healthy, and that the fee fits your budget. Our [mortgage calculator](/mortgage) can help you factor the fee into your monthly cost.

title: Buyer Agreements and Agent Commissions: What Changed and What It Means for You
excerpt: Since August 2024, buyers sign a written agreement with their agent before touring homes. Here's what that agreement covers and the questions to ask.
content:
If you're starting a home search, you'll notice one change from how things used to work: before you tour a home with an agent, you'll be asked to sign a written agreement. That's the result of industry practice changes that took effect on August 17, 2024. Here's what changed, what the agreement covers, and what to ask before you sign.

**What Changed in 2024**
Two practice changes affect buyers most:
- Written agreements before touring: agents working with buyers through the MLS must have a written agreement with the buyer before touring a home, in person or virtually.
- Compensation offers moved off the MLS: listings can no longer advertise an offer to pay the buyer's agent. Sellers can still choose to pay a buyer's agent, and that's now worked out directly between the parties.

Sellers can still offer concessions, such as help with a buyer's closing costs, and those can be shown on the MLS.

**What the Written Agreement Covers**
A buyer agreement spells out the working relationship:
- The services your agent will provide
- How your agent is compensated, stated as a specific amount or rate, and how it's earned
- How long the agreement lasts, and whether it covers specific homes, specific towns, or your whole search
- Whether it's exclusive, meaning you work only with that agent for its term
- How either side can end it

Commissions are not set by law and are negotiable. The agreement has to state that clearly, and the amount your agent receives can't exceed what's in the agreement.

**Who Pays the Buyer's Agent?**
It can be paid in a few ways. A seller may agree to pay the buyer's agent, either as a policy for their listing or because you ask for it in your offer. If the seller pays less than what's in your agreement, or nothing, you'd owe the difference under the terms you agreed to. Some buyers ask the seller for a concession toward their costs instead. Your agent should walk you through how each option affects your offer before you write one.

**Questions to Ask Before You Sign**
- How long does this agreement last, and can I shorten it?
- Is it for one home, one town, or my entire search?
- What happens if I want to end the agreement early?
- What services are included, and is anything extra?
- If the seller offers to pay part or all of your compensation, how is that handled?
- If I find a home on my own, or through an open house, does the agreement still apply?

A clear agreement protects you as much as the agent. If anything is unclear, ask for it to be explained or changed in writing before you sign.

**Touring Without an Agreement**
You can still visit open houses on your own, and you can contact a listing agent directly about a home. The written agreement requirement applies when you work with an agent to tour homes on your behalf.

**Frequently Asked Questions**

Do I have to sign a buyer agreement to see a house? If an agent is showing you homes, yes. Agents who use the MLS need a written agreement before touring with you. You can still attend open houses without one.

Can I negotiate my agent's commission? Yes. Commissions are not set by law and are always negotiable.

Will I have to pay my agent out of pocket? Only if the seller doesn't cover your agent's compensation and your agreement says you're responsible for it. Many buyers ask the seller to cover it as part of their offer.

Can I sign an agreement for just one home? Often, yes. Agreements can be limited to a specific property, a set time period, or a specific area. Ask for the scope that fits how you want to work.

Does this change anything for sellers? Sellers no longer see compensation offers on the MLS, so they decide directly whether to offer anything to a buyer's agent, or respond to what a buyer asks for. Our guide to [what it costs to sell a home in Massachusetts](/blog/cost-to-sell-home-massachusetts) covers the seller side.
